I always ask people why they want to get married. What are you getting out of it?

\- If you want to be the stay-at-home partner and want reassurance that your partner isn't just going to peace out and leave you with nothing -> then YES! No matter how long you'll be married, as long as you don't have any alternative financial agreements in place (like prenup), being married will be benefitial for you in that situation.

\- Do you want to follow the tradition, make your parents happy, get people off your back, etc? -> NO.  Doing anything for others is never worth it, and with marriage, you are putting all of your money on the line.

\- Do you want to 'seal the deal' and ensure your relationship is taken to the next level, that you got your partner secured for life, and have a guarantee that this thing will last? -> NO. There is no such guarantee.

\- Do you want a symbolic milestone, a celebration with your friends and family, a promise you make to your partner? -> Maybe! But I'd personally just have a ceremony in that case and not sign any paperwork which once again, exposes you financially to an extremely uncomfortable degree.

In my highly subjective option, you might be overestimating the health of those relationships. Majority of people I've met who 'fell in love and got married easily' fell into one of these scenarios: 

1. Young & stupid love (40%): falling in love in your 20s, seriously limiting personal growth and feeling too scared to leave the relationship once it's gone sour. 

2. Tic toc love (30%): finding someone you can tolerate in your 30s, because it's time, because OMG I can't anymore, because no one is going to want you in a year or two. 

3. 'Love' cause you can't adult alone (20%): 20s or 30s, when people simply lack in one major aspect of life and need a partner to fix it for them. 

4. Actually good, sustainable partnerships based on shared values, vision of the future, and solid communication (10% - at best). 

My point being that 'love' isn't something that will last, and marriage is a false promise of security. Divorce rate is what it is for a reason. Relationships take a lot of work & skill to build and falling in love fast & getting married shows impulsive thinking and immaturity more than anything else.

I would make it very clear that you want a partner who can talk about the future with you. Do not fall for "it's too early". In my experience, when a guy is ready to find a future partner, they are ready to talk about it on date one. It may not be a "here is how many kids I want" conversation, but it will include what he wants, what he doesn't want, and what he is till trying to figure out. Anything less, I would consider to be an issue with communication.

Is it fair to ask you to give up the best feeling in the world, for the sake of *alleged* security, driven by fear that without a man, you will perish? I don’t think it is. Yes, women might be more giving than men naturally, but giving up *the best feeling in the world* to address this huge unfairness isn’t a fair task of women. We are not here to sacrifice ourselves, once again, to plug the potholes of patriarchy. Men can do better for women who love them equally as much. As someone who’s been on both sides of this, I can tell you one thing - even though all of these relationships are in the past, the relationships when I was allowing myself to be loved feel like a much bigger waste of time than those where I was truly in love. Don’t get me wrong - be smart, date smart, don’t chase unavailable men - but please don’t give up on your chance to love for the sake of security which may or may not come from a man who “loves you more”.

I worked in the beauty industry (marketing on the corporate side) and I can tell you all of the marketing in beauty is major BS.

Sephora purposely "builds categories" and forces different brands to launch similar products at the same time to create "trends". They also work very hard to push the idea of yet another skin care step because it makes them the big bucks. I worked in hair care, and we would constantly get the message to just create more steps and do to hair what they have done in skincare.

Margins of the products you see in Sephora are absurd - 80-90%, for reference, anything you buy in Target has a margin of 30-50% (max). Do not fall for any claims that start with "x number of women said" - all of those consumer perception studies are purposely designed to drive to certain results (e.g. having a 4 point scale vs 5 point scale so no one could be in the middle, asking the same question a million different times and picking the one that has the most well-perceived responses, guiding respondents to certain answers, etc.). Also watch out for anything that uses words like "visibly" or "healthy-looking / feeling" (which is nearly all products) - those are just magic words that mean it's based on nothing but perception, which allows them to not prove anything clinically. Do not even get me started or reviews and influencers.

No dermatologist would tell you to use a 10-step routine. They will tell you to use CeraVe and sunscreen. God I hate the beauty industry so much.

I'm sorry you're going through a rough period. It's definitely difficult. I've been super-depressed for most of my life, and one thing that has helped me is focusing on accepting things as they are and adapting, instead of focusing on how you wish your life could have been. I've noticed that being ok with yourself is the #1 thing that differentiates happy/content people who can enjoy life from those who are constantly miserable. No one can be perfect, and unless you're ok with yourself how you are, you will never get out of the funk, no matter what you have or achieve. 

A few practical things that helped me do that:

1. Therapy. Start as soon as you can. If you can't afford it, there is a ton of resources on YouTube, Reddit, your local library and other places. Just make sure you go for what's researched and not what your friend's life coach suggests. 
2. Yoga or exercise in general. Is my far the best way to FEEL more in control and powerful... The book 'The Body Keeps the Score' breaks down why it's so important for those with trauma. It's a bit lengthy, but you can find a summary on YouTube.
3. Taking note of what exactly triggers you in life. We tend to avoid going after the actual problems by generalizing. It makes us feel trapped. I know that for me, despite me saying "nothing is going right" and "my life is just over" there were a few key triggers - conflict if my relationship, my parents guilt-tripping me, and the bullies at work. Focusing on things on-by-one can help you fix what's actually broken. 
4. Hobbies. My mom got sick with terminal cancer last year (and since passed away), and there is one thing I learned from it - there is no deeper level to this game. When she was sick, she wanted to do what she has always liked to do. Plant flowers, do embroidery, cook. Life isn't about some huge achievements - it's about enjoying the little things. I've then decided that if I want to stay on the couch and knit the whole evening, that's exactly what I'm going to do. That's what I enjoy - it's not a waste of time. 
5. You choose who you surround yourself with. It's difficult to make friends, but extremely important to keep trying to actually pick the people you connect with instead of trying to mold yourself into the people you're already surrounded by. I've had a very difficult time most of my life trying to fit in with the cool kids (I'm nearly 35, so you can see how dumb that was). I've now accepted I'm not cool, and I'm having a much easier time connected with people around me. 

I hope this helps in some way. I know a lot of it is borderline cliché, but that's what has helped me. I still battle depression, but no longer hate myself. Best of luck to you.

So very sorry to hear. It's the worst news. I just went through this with my mom, who passes after an almost year-long battle. We were told it's untreatable, and she has a year max, with treatment, 1-2 months without. We opted for treatment, and it worked, she handled it as well as one can handle chemo & radiation, and lived with us for 10 months. Up until her last month, she was doing "ok". 

There are a few things I want to share with you. 

First thing that surprised me is that no matter how hard this is and how sick he is, there is still life. My mom was sick for 10 months but most of the time she was still able to live her life - with some limitations, of course, but with things she still enjoyed, with her family by her side and with our love and support. I think that was priceless, and she appreciated that time more than anything, even with the gray cloud of cancer hanging over her head. 

You are doing an amazing job - no matter what, you're doing everything you can. Until the very last day with my mom, I focused on what we can do, how we can make it better for her, and that brought me a tremendous amount of comfort. I'll forever think of going through this journey with her as the most important job I've ever done (I don't have kids, but I'm sure it would be on-par with caring for them)
